I've finished the change to how people sign in, and it's ready for you to look at. The old login code kept the session in two places, a cookie and a table in the database, and the two could disagree. That's why some people were signed out at random after a deploy. Now the session lives only in the database, and the cookie just holds a random key that points to it. I wrote a migration that copies the live sessions across, so nobody gets signed out when this goes out. It ran on a copy of last night's data in about forty seconds, and it moved every session it found. The tests all pass, and I added eleven new ones for the cases that broke before. One of them signs in, restarts the server, and checks that the session is still there. Another one signs in on two devices and signs out on one of them. I also tried it by hand in the browser, on the desktop and on a phone, and both behaved as they should. There's one thing I'm not sure about. The session now expires after thirty days of no activity, where before it never expired at all. That's safer, but some people may be surprised when they have to sign in again next month. If you'd rather keep the old behaviour for now, it's a one line change, and I can make it before you merge. The other open question is the admin panel. It still reads the old cookie directly, so it will keep working until we remove that cookie, but it won't see the new sessions. I'd like to move it over next, which should take about an hour. Nothing has been pushed yet. The branch is called session cleanup, and the pull request explains each step and why. Tell me whether to keep the thirty day expiry, and whether I should start on the admin panel.

The nightly import failed again, and this time I found out why. The supplier changed their export last Tuesday, and every date now comes with a time zone at the end. Our parser didn't expect that, so it threw away about one row in six without saying anything. The import still reported success, because it only counted the rows it kept. That's the part that worries me most, so I fixed it first. The import now stops and reports an error if it skips more than one row in a thousand, and the report says which rows and why. Then I taught the parser to read the new format, and to keep reading the old one, since the archive files still use it. I ran the whole of last month through it again. It took about twelve minutes, and it recovered four thousand two hundred rows that had gone missing. The totals now match the supplier's own summary to the cent, for every day I checked. There were two days where they didn't match at first. Both turned out to be refunds that were booked on the wrong day at their end, so I left those alone and wrote them down in the notes. I also added a test that feeds in a file with the new dates, one with the old dates, and one with a mix of both. All three pass. Before you run it on the real database, there's one decision for you. The missing rows include orders that were already shipped, and adding them now will change last month's numbers in the finance report. If finance has already closed the month, they may want the corrections booked this month instead. I can do it either way, with a small flag on the command. Do you want me to fill in last month as it was, or book the corrections into this month?

I looked into why the plots were hard to read on your phone, and the short answer is that the labels are too long for the space they get. With seventeen bars, each bar gets about fifty pixels, and some labels need more than two hundred. The page squeezes them together until they overlap. I tried three fixes on the same data. The first was to show fewer bars, the top eight, and put the rest under a heading called other. That reads well, but you lose detail you might want. The second was to turn the chart on its side, so the labels sit on the left with room to breathe. That kept every bar readable on a narrow screen, and it's what most dashboards do. The third was to shorten the labels automatically, which saved space but made several of them ambiguous, so I'd drop that one. I went with the second, and I added a check that runs whenever the agent draws a plot. The check draws the chart on the server, measures every label, and complains if any two of them touch or run off the edge. It found the same problem on four of the existing plots, and it passes on all of them now. It doesn't need a browser, so it adds no new dependency, and it takes about a third of a second per plot. What it can't do is tell whether a chart looks good. It only catches the problems we taught it, like overlap and clipping. If you want the agent to judge the whole picture, we'd need to send it an image of the plot, which is a bigger job and costs more per run. The test run that would show whether the agent follows the new rule costs about four dollars. Should I run it now?

The release is out, but it took longer than planned, so here's what happened. The build started at nine and failed twenty minutes later, because the cache on the build server had filled the disk. I cleared the old images, which freed about forty gigabytes, and the second build went through cleanly. The tests passed on the first try. Then the deploy stopped halfway, because the certificate for the staging server had expired on Sunday. Nobody noticed, since nothing calls staging over the weekend. I renewed it, and I set up a reminder that warns two weeks before the next one runs out. After that, the rollout went to one server first, as usual. Error rates stayed flat for fifteen minutes, so I let it go to the rest. Everything has been on the new version since a quarter past eleven. Response times are about the same as before, and a little faster on the search page. There is one thing I'd like you to know about. During the half hour when staging was broken, two scheduled jobs tried to run there and failed. They're the weekly cleanup and the usage report. Neither does anything urgent, and I've started both again by hand, but the usage report will arrive a day late. I've written up the timeline in the release notes, with the times and what I did at each step. Two changes would stop this from happening again. One is to clean the build cache every week, which is a small job I can add today. The other is to move all our certificates to automatic renewal, which needs access to the domain settings, so I'd need you to give me that. Would you like me to do both, or only the cache cleanup for now?
